clue.text: Concise way to describe neat

definitions.meaning: brief and to the point, with nothing wasted
a neat spirit is a short drink, and neat also once meant pleasing or nice, so the pair describes it

explanation.walkthrough: A double definition: the phrase for brevity, and a playful description of 'neat' as two adjectives, a short drink and something pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means brief and pleasantly so, which is what a concise remark is.

clue.text: Maybe that sand's able to support tiles!

definitions.text: Maybe that sand's able to support tiles!

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be otherwise arranged, so the words that follow are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words, including the S of the contraction, form the pool

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether sand is firm enough to hold up roof tiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiles' is old slang for hats, so the whole clue describes hall furniture on which hats hang, while the anagram of THATSANDS spells it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stands for hats hold up headgear, which slang calls tiles.

clue.text: A ruler in the East breaks cane, resulting in temporary inactivity.

parts.note: a bey was a governor or ruler in the Ottoman Empire

indicators.note: breaks tells us the word cane is broken up and its letters reassembled

explanation.surface: An Eastern potentate snaps a cane, and everything grinds to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' looks like a verb acting on the ruler, but it signals the anagram; a bey was a provincial governor in the Ottoman Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in abeyance is suspended for the time being, dormant until revived.

indicators.note: comes first says the rain piece is placed at the front, before the autumn piece

parts.note: fall is the American word for autumn

explanation.surface: In autumn, a downpour of rain comes before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names autumn before rain, but 'comes first' puts the rain word in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A waterfall is a cascade of water over a drop, a synonym pairing.

clue.text: Dance held on public property? regular old time with it?

definitions.meaning: a measure is a stately dance, and a common is land owned by the public
in music, ... is the regular four-beat time, an old name for common time

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading jokes that a measure (dance) on a common is the phrase; the second is the musical term. 'with it?' joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical name for four-four time, the most regular metre, is the same phrase.

clue.text: The man's belt is buckled: means business, I reckon!

indicators.note: buckled means bent out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these words, including the S, go into the pool

explanation.surface: Someone notices a bent belt buckle and concludes the wearer means business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buckled' looks like fastening the belt, but it signals that THEMANSBELT is rearranged. 'means' and 'I reckon' are link padding.
explanation.definitionFit: An establishment is a business premises or firm.

clue.text: Accompanying horsemen -faster than the rest

definitions.meaning: mounted attendants who ride beside or ahead of a carriage
those who outride others, outpacing the field

explanation.walkthrough: A double definition: the escort riders, and a literal reading of the word as those who out-ride everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Escort riders accompanying a vehicle are its outriders.

clue.text: Trials for big games.

definitions.meaning: Test matches are the major international fixtures in cricket

explanation.walkthrough: TESTS are the full international matches in cricket and rugby, the biggest games of the season.
explanation.definitionFit: Trials and examinations are synonyms; Test matches are the top international fixtures.

clue.text: Kind of steam ship officers.

indicators.note: kind of hints at a variety or version of the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of steamship officers serve on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of steam ship' reads as a steamship, but 'Kind of' rearranges STEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Mates are the deck officers below the captain on a merchant vessel.

clue.text: No amount of that kind is unique

parts.note: none means not any, no amount at all
such means of that sort or kind

explanation.surface: Something is so rare that there is no other of its kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaically used as an adjective, it means without equal or peerless.

clue.text: Despatched men in it with some feeling.

indicators.note: in says the men word goes inside the word it

explanation.surface: Soldiers despatched to war go with some emotion.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentiment is a feeling or emotion, a synonym.

clue.text: Negligent in the occasional sense?

definitions.meaning: ... work or labour is irregular, taken up now and then

explanation.walkthrough: 'in the occasional sense' tells the solver to take the word as in casual labour, done now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless and offhand describe a casual attitude; casual jobs are occasional.

clue.text: Pledge yourself to deal with grave business?

definitions.meaning: to promise or commit oneself to a task
to act as a funeral director, an ..., who deals with graves

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition jokes that an undertaker's job is to 'undertake' burials.
explanation.definitionFit: To commit oneself to doing something is to promise it.

clue.text: Thus love is taken in abroad that's certainly ironical

indicators.note: is taken in says the thus-and-love pieces are enclosed by the abroad word

parts.note: forth means out and abroad, as in to go forth
so means thus, in this way
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone abroad finds love and declares it, with a touch of irony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' looks like a location but gives FORTH, which takes in SO and O.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic interjection meaning truly is now used mockingly, a certainly said ironically.

clue.text: Member of religious fraternity direction seen to be different.

indicators.note: different suggests the letters are made to differ from their order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: SE is south-east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A monk looks in another direction and sees things differently.
explanation.definitionFit: The Essenes were an ancient Jewish ascetic brotherhood, a religious fraternity.

explanation.definitionFit: Robinson Crusoe is the famous fictional castaway of Defoe's novel.

clue.text: Dreadful when it's legal to be decapitated!.

indicators.note: decapitated means the head is cut off, so the first letter of the synonym goes

parts.note: legal means lawful, allowed by law

explanation.walkthrough: 'to be decapitated' removes the first letter of the synonym of legal.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful and dreadful are synonyms meaning terrible.

clue.text: Dear me! The alternative coach has to be used.

parts.note: tut is an exclamation of mild disapproval, like dear me

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in dismay that the other coach must be used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' suggests a bus, but here it means teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach and a tutor both give private instruction, synonyms.

clue.text: Weapon of plunder.

definitions.meaning: to ransack or search and steal

explanation.definitionFit: A gun with a grooved barrel is one weapon; ransacking is the verb.

clue.text: Not ready to get really fit, so puts up a poor performance on the track.

definitions.text: Not ready to get really fit, so puts up a poor performance on the track.

parts.words: Not ready to get really fit, so puts up a poor performance on the track.
parts.note: reads like an unfit athlete slow to get into shape and losing races, but describes a stopping railway service that is slow on its rails

explanation.surface: An athlete reluctant to get in shape performs badly on the running track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'track' means railway track, not an athletics track, and 'slow to train' becomes the name of a stopping service.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopping service on the railway is slow, a poor performer on the line.

clue.text: Nags on which most people are to put their shirts?

definitions.text: Nags on which most people are to put their shirts?

parts.words: Nags on which most people are to put their shirts?
parts.note: putting one's shirt on a horse means betting everything on it, but here shirts literally go on a drying frame

explanation.walkthrough: To put your shirt on a horse is a British idiom for betting all you have; the frames are nags only in jest.
explanation.definitionFit: Frames for drying laundry hold shirts, punningly called horses.
